facts.text: President Donald Trump signed two executive orders restricting birthright citizenship on Thursday.
The Supreme Court ruled in June, by a 6-3 vote and two months before the new orders, that Trump's birthright citizenship policy could not stand and that birthright citizenship remained the law.
One executive order expands or narrows the categories of non-citizens whose children would not be eligible for birthright citizenship.
The second executive order prohibits "birth tourism," defined as pregnant women or visitors travelling to the US on visas to give birth so their children obtain US citizenship.
Trump criticized the Supreme Court's birthright citizenship decision, calling it unfortunate, bad and unfair.
Trump signed an executive order seeking to end birthright citizenship at the start of his second term in early 2025.

Stephen Miller, homeland security advisor and White House deputy chief of staff for policy, said one order would deny birthright citizenship to children of members of "foreign terrorist organizations," alien enemies of the United States, and people who lobby or act on behalf of foreign governments.
Miller said birth tourism is banned as of the signing of the second executive order and that no one may obtain a visa for that purpose.

Miller cited section 215(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows the president to set exceptions and limitations on entry into the country, as the source of the president's authority to ban birth tourism.
Trump said hundreds of thousands of babies have been born in the US through birth tourism, speaking from the Oval Office.

Iran is seeking to bar U.S. ships from the Strait of Hormuz, and disclosed details of an agreement with Oman concerning the reopening of the strait, while Trump faces pressure to reach a breakthrough with Iran.

Birthright citizenship is established in the 14th Amendment of the US Constitution, which grants citizenship to children born in the United States with narrow exceptions such as children of foreign diplomats or members of an enemy occupying force.

The first executive order bars automatic citizenship for babies born in the US to two non-citizen parents when one parent is a member of a foreign terrorist group, a foreign government employee, has attempted to obtain citizenship fraudulently, or lives in a US territory where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute.
Miller said obtaining a visa for the purpose of giving birth in the United States constitutes fraud against the U.S. government.
Miller said some people enter the US as tourists or visitors with the intention of having a child who becomes an automatic citizen.
There are no official figures on the number of foreigners who travel to the United States specifically to give birth and obtain citizenship.
The Center for Immigration Studies states that between 20,000 and 25,000 mothers traveled to the United States to give birth in 2016-2017.

The Migration Policy Institute said the most expansive census-based estimate places birth tourism births in the US at about 22,000 to 26,000 per year, and that government data showed 9,600 births in 2024 to mothers with foreign addresses.

Solicitor General John Sauer said during Supreme Court oral arguments in April that "no one knows for sure" the extent of the practice, and referenced media reports estimating more than 1.1 million, and 1.5 million from the People's Republic of China alone.
The White House stated that the new executive orders do not conflict with the Supreme Court ruling.
A federal regulation implemented in 2020 during Trump's first term prohibits the use of temporary tourist and business visas primarily to obtain US citizenship for a newborn.

Gabriel Chin, a law professor at the University of California Davis, said parts of the order raise constitutional questions and that the president lacks power to declare a child born in the US not a citizen.
The new executive orders contain narrower restrictions than Trump's earlier measures.
Birthright citizenship in US territories such as Puerto Rico is established by federal statute.
NBC News correspondent Gabe Gutierrez reported on the executive orders in a 1 minute 51 second segment on NBC's Nightly News, published Aug. 6, 2026.

facts.text: A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta to pay $567 million (€492 million / £421 million).
The $567 million order was in addition to $375 million in damages previously ordered by a jury in the same case, bringing Meta's total New Mexico liability to $942 million.

The money is to be placed in a fund intended to reduce future harms, with about three-quarters ($420 million), payable over five years, designated for mental health treatment and clinical and behavioural health programmes for young people, and the remainder going to prevention programs, screening and related services.

The judge ordered Meta to prevent accounts of users under 18 from being recommended to adults and to prevent adults from messaging underage users.

Tennessee Republicans passed a congressional map in May that redrew Cohen's Memphis-based district to lean more Republican; the district previously had a majority Black population.
The redrawn 9th district extends across more than half of Tennessee's southern border, roughly 200 miles (320km) east from Memphis, and north into Middle Tennessee toward Nashville.
Shelby County, which contains Memphis, is divided among three congressional districts under the new map.
Brent Taylor defeated Republican primary challengers Charlotte Bergmann, Jeremy Thompson and state Rep. Todd Warner.
Justin Pearson defeated Democratic primary candidates Jim Torino, state Sen. London Lamar and M. LaTroya A-Williams.
Rep. Steve Cohen (D) is retiring and said he would not seek reelection because of the new congressional lines.

According to The Downballot, Tennessee's 9th Congressional District, covering the southwestern corner of the state around Memphis, voted for former Vice President Harris by 21 percentage points in 2024.
A federal judge panel allowed Tennessee Republicans to use the new map for the midterm elections.
According to an Associated Press estimate, 71% of voters in the new 9th district are new to the district.
Charlie Hatcher, a former Tennessee agriculture commissioner, defeated Republican Rep. Andy Ogles in the 5th congressional district primary.
Donald Trump had endorsed Andy Ogles early in the primary.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee endorsed Charlie Hatcher.
The FBI seized Andy Ogles's cellphone in 2024 during an investigation into his campaign finance reporting, and the justice department agreed to return it.
Senator Marsha Blackburn won the Republican primary for governor of Tennessee.
Memphis city council member Jerri Green won the Democratic primary for governor of Tennessee.
Bill Lee is prevented by term limits from seeking reelection as governor.
